messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Patel was 29 when he came to treatment, a married man who worked as a house painter, spending most days moving between apartment buildings, renovation sites, and private homes with drop cloths, ladders, and paint-splattered work pants. The robbery had happened eight months earlier, at the end of a long workday. He had been carrying his tools and the week’s cash payment as he walked past a row of storefronts on a route he had taken many times. He still spoke about that block as if it held a charge. Even before he could describe the whole event, he could describe the location with precision—the narrow stretch of sidewalk, the recessed doorway, the alley opening beside it. Those physical places had become potent for him, not as abstract reminders but as exact spaces his body reacted to.

He remembered a man stepping into his path and another coming from the side. After that, the memory became jagged. Arjun would say he knew there had been shouting, a hand grabbing at him, the sickening realization that he was trapped between them, but he could not put the sequence together in a way that felt complete. When he tried to recount it deliberately for his wife or later in therapy, he would stall and look confused, as if the memory broke apart the harder he reached for it. What came most sharply were fragments: the scrape of his shoes against the pavement, the feel of his bag being yanked, the sense of being watched and overpowered. Alongside those flashes came a rush of guilt that made his face tighten. He had come to believe he should have done something differently—crossed the street sooner, noticed them earlier, protected the money, fought back harder. Even though he knew he had been outnumbered, when the memory surged up he felt accused by it.

In the weeks after the robbery, the event returned to him suddenly, without warning. He could be rolling paint onto a wall and, for a second, be right back on that sidewalk. Sometimes it happened when he passed similar storefronts for work; sometimes the trigger was waking in the dark from a nightmare with his heart pounding before he was fully awake. On those mornings he lay rigid in bed, already braced, listening for sounds in the apartment. His wife would ask what was wrong, and he often told her it was nothing, but he would get up feeling as if danger had started before sunrise. He described his body as never really settling. His shoulders stayed tight, his jaw clenched, and even routine errands felt like situations he had to prepare for physically.

That constant readiness followed him into his work. Because painters spend time entering unfamiliar buildings and moving through hallways, stairwells, and back entrances, Arjun found himself checking every corner and doorway before he focused on the job. He watched people’s hands, their distance from him, the ways they approached. If he heard footsteps behind him while carrying supplies, he turned immediately. Coworkers had begun to notice that he startled into anger. If someone came up too quickly or joked about him being jumpy, he snapped back hard. At home, too, his wife had seen him become irritable in ways that were new for him—short-tempered over small interruptions, sharp in tone, quick to assume bad intentions. He did not experience this as overreaction. From his point of view, being on guard was what made sense now. He was certain that people could not be trusted, and the robbery had settled into him as proof that anyone could turn on you if they saw an opportunity.

Over the following months, Arjun quietly narrowed his world. He took longer routes to avoid the block where he had been robbed and tried to decline jobs in that neighborhood when he could, which was not always possible in his line of work. When he had to go near similar locations, he arrived already tense and distracted, scanning constantly rather than talking with clients or coworkers. He shared less with friends and family because he felt set apart from them, as if other people moved through the city with an ease that no longer belonged to him. Their reassurances did not land. He had come to feel that relying on others was naïve; even asking for help seemed foolish if, in the end, no one could really keep him safe.

What finally brought him to seek treatment was not one dramatic crisis but the accumulation of strain. His wife told him she felt shut out and was worried by how angry and distant he had become. At work, a supervisor commented on his temper after he barked at a coworker who had approached him from behind on a job site. Arjun arrived for help exhausted by nights broken by nightmares and by days spent keyed up and watchful. What frightened him most was the sense that the robbery still lived in his body and in certain places, and that he no longer knew how to be around people without expecting something from them. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not to erase what happened but to stop feeling as if every sidewalk, every doorway, and every waking from sleep might lead him back there again.
